# (Example Client) ISO 42001 Project Brief

**Analyst Orientation | Certification readiness and gap closure | 2026-2027**

> **TLDR:** Help (Example Client) turn an existing set of AI practices and technical controls into a complete, auditable AI management system (AIMS).

## 1. Client Overview

- (Example Client) is a 160+ person digital-services company founded in 2017. It researches, designs, builds, and modernizes digital products and services.
- Its work spans government, nonprofit, and selected commercial partners, with a strong focus on public-interest technology, healthcare, and Veterans services.
- Publicly identified government customers and partners include the Department of Veterans Affairs, CMS/HHS, IRS, OPM, and other federal programs.
- The company combines product management, research, design, engineering, strategy, and delivery services.

## 2. AI Usage

- (Example Client) is actively adopting and designing AI technology and has published Responsible AI principles centered on stewardship, intentionality, human agency, impact, accountability, privacy, and security.
- The certification scope is focused on the Innovation and Platform teams' building and provision of AI products - not the entire company's general end-user AI use.
- Their documents describe 4 AI systems, 9 SDLC AI tools, 10 infrastructure services, a model registry, and a 19-item gap register.
- Engineering controls already described include gated evaluation metrics, human approval gates, provenance hashing, fail-closed defaults, production telemetry, PR/CI review, prompt/version controls, and immutable image digests.

## 3. What is already in place

| Foundation | Examples |
|---|---|
| Scope & inventory | Draft AIMS scope; AI systems/tools/infrastructure inventory; model registry. |
| Risk | 20 AI-category risks in Drata with owners, treatments, residual scores, and open actions. |
| Engineering | Lifecycle testing, monitoring, change controls, human approval, agent authority limits. |
| Existing governance | SOC 2 policy suite, enterprise risk process, incident management, vendor program, quarterly leadership review. |
| Corporate AI baseline | Responsible AI Principles and company-wide AI Use Policy for end-user use. |

## 4. Gap Analysis

> Treat client readiness statements as hypotheses until evidence shows the control is documented, implemented, evidenced, and operating.

| Area | What to verify / close |
|---|---|
| AIMS governance | No producer-scope AIMS AI policy yet; scope draft still needs leadership approval. |
| Impact assessment | No AI impact assessments have been completed; methodology/template must be established and used. |
| Training & competence | AI-specific training is planned but not yet operating. |
| Data governance | Existing classification taxonomy does not yet cover AI artifacts such as corpora, datasets, checkpoints, and delivered models. |
| AI suppliers | AI-specific suppliers have not yet been run through the existing vendor program; supplier contract/DPA requirements are incomplete. |
| Control codification | Some human-review and engineering practices operate in code/process but are not fully reflected in policy text. |
| Regulatory mapping | Formal per-market AI regulatory/contractual mapping has not yet been performed. |
| Internal audit | No standalone AI/AIMS internal audit program or completed AI-scoped internal audit exists. |
| Management review | AI is discussed in quarterly leadership review, but a dedicated standing AI/AIMS review structure needs to be formalized. |

### Analyst evidence test

- **Documented** — Is the requirement formally defined?
- **Implemented** — Is the process actually in use?
- **Evidence exists** — Can (Example Client) produce records showing execution?
- **Tested** — Does sampling/interview evidence support consistent operation?

## 6. Needs

- Maintain the clause/control mapping, evidence index, remediation tracker, owner, due date, and status.
- Review submitted evidence against the four-part evidence test; flag unsupported or ambiguous readiness claims.
- Draft and revise policies, procedures, templates, and workpapers for lead review - do not invent operating practices.
- Support AI impact assessments and supplier reviews by gathering evidence, pre-populating factual sections, and tracking actions.
- Prepare test samples, record objective evidence, and document exceptions for the internal audit.
- Organize Stage 1/Stage 2 evidence so an auditor can trace each requirement to a current, approved artifact or record.

### Working rule

> If a control is described but you cannot trace it to an owner, current artifact, and operating evidence, treat it as unresolved and escalate it to the engagement lead.

## 7. ISO Requirements

- AIMS scope, governance, objectives, policies, roles, and responsibilities are approved and understood.
- AI inventory, risks, impact assessments, supplier controls, lifecycle controls, and training are current and evidenced.
- Required processes have operated long enough to produce credible records for auditor sampling.
- Internal audit has tested the AIMS; findings have owners and corrective actions.
- Management review has considered AIMS performance, risks, audit results, changes, resources, and improvement actions.
- Stage 1 findings are closed or controlled before Stage 2; process owners can explain what they do and show evidence.

## 8. Engagement Guardrails

- 200 total consulting hours: protect time for January testing and certification support.
- (Example Client) owns implementation and evidence production; our team structures, reviews, tests, and challenges.
- Use existing SOC 2 processes where they genuinely satisfy AIMS requirements rather than creating parallel processes.
- Prefer durable, auditable processes over one-time documents created solely for certification.
- Escalate scope changes, major control redesign, legal/contract questions, or unsupported high-risk claims to the engagement lead.

## 9. Key Risks

- Overstated readiness or evidence that reflects design rather than operation.
- Late implementation that leaves too little operating history before Stage 2.
- Slow SME responses, policy approvals, vendor reviews, or contract decisions.
- Internal-audit or management-review slippage.
- Scope creep consuming the 200-hour budget.
- Certification-body scheduling or findings pushing issuance into April.
